# Chapter 12 Practice: Physical Properties of Solutions

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/solutions.md`), grouped by objective. 27 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1a}} · *short answer* A student keeps adding salt to a glass of water. After a certain point, salt crystals sit undissolved on the bottom no matter how long the glass is stirred. What term describes this solution, and why?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Saturated.** The solution has reached the maximum amount of salt that can dissolve in that volume of water at that temperature — any additional salt simply cannot dissolve, which is exactly why undissolved crystals remain visible regardless of stirring.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1a}} · *conceptual* Dissolving ammonium nitrate ($\ce{NH4NO3}$) in water causes the resulting solution to feel noticeably cold — this is the basis of instant cold packs. Is this dissolution process exothermic or endothermic? Explain in terms of the three interactions involved.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Endothermic.** The new solute-solvent (ion-dipole) attraction between $\ce{NH4NO3}$'s ions and water is weaker than the solvent-solvent (hydrogen bonding) and solute-solute (ionic lattice) attractions it replaces, so net energy must be absorbed from the surroundings — cooling the pack.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1a}} · *multiple-choice* Which of these is NOT one of the six common solution types?

(A) A gas dissolved in a solid
(B) A solid dissolved in a solid
\(C) A solid dissolved in a gas
(D) A gas dissolved in a liquid
:::
::: tab Answer
**\(C)** A solid genuinely dissolved in a gas is not one of the six standard types. Gases have essentially no intermolecular attraction to offer a solute, so there is nothing to hold dissolved solid particles apart — solid particles suspended in air (smoke, dust) form a *suspension* or *aerosol*, which is heterogeneous, not a homogeneous solution.

The other three are all real: **(A)** hydrogen absorbed in palladium, **(B)** brass (zinc in copper), **(D)** carbonated water.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1b}} · *multiple-choice* Which solvent would dissolve naphthalene (a nonpolar solid) better?

(A) Water (polar)
(B) Hexane (nonpolar)
\(C) Both equally well
(D) Neither
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B)** "Like dissolves like" — naphthalene is nonpolar, so it is far more soluble in nonpolar hexane than in polar water.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1b}} · *short answer* Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why oil and vinegar (mostly water) separate into two layers instead of mixing into one solution.
:::
::: tab Answer
Oil is nonpolar (dispersion forces only) while vinegar is polar (dominated by water's hydrogen bonding). These intermolecular forces are incompatible — oil molecules cannot participate in water's hydrogen-bonding network — so the two liquids are not miscible and remain as separate layers.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1b}} · *short answer* Soap molecules have a long hydrocarbon chain ending in a charged $\ce{-COO^-}$ head. Use "like dissolves like" to explain how a single soap molecule can help grease dissolve in water.
:::
::: tab Answer
A soap molecule is deliberately built to be "like" **both** solvents at once, in different regions.

- The **long hydrocarbon tail** is nonpolar and dissolves readily into nonpolar grease, held there by dispersion forces.
- The **charged $\ce{-COO^-}$ head** is strongly attracted to polar water by ion-dipole forces.

Many soap molecules surround a grease droplet with their tails buried in the grease and their heads pointing outward. The resulting sphere — a **micelle** — presents an entirely charged surface to the water, so the water treats it as it would any ionic solute and carries it away.

This is the same reasoning as the alcohol series in the study guide, but exploited on purpose: instead of one part winning, soap keeps the two parts far enough apart that each does its own job.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1c}} · *workout* The solubility of $\ce{O2}$ gas in water at 25 °C and 1.00 atm is 0.041 M. Estimate its solubility at a partial pressure of 0.21 atm (approximately its partial pressure in air).
:::
::: tab Answer
By Henry's law, solubility is directly proportional to pressure:

$$0.041\ \text{M} \times \frac{0.21\ \text{atm}}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 8.6\times10^{-3}\ \text{M}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1c}} · *short answer* A can of soda goes flat noticeably faster once opened and left at room temperature versus kept sealed in the refrigerator. Explain this using two separate solubility principles from this chapter.
:::
::: tab Answer
Opening the can drops the pressure above the liquid, and by Henry's law, lower pressure means lower $\ce{CO2}$ solubility — CO₂ escapes as bubbles. Separately, warming the soda (leaving it at room temperature) further lowers gas solubility, since gas solubility always decreases as temperature increases. Both effects push dissolved $\ce{CO2}$ out of solution.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 12.1c}} · *workout* At 25 °C the solubility of $\ce{O2}$ in water is $1.3\times10^{-3}$ M when the partial pressure of $\ce{O2}$ above the water is 1.00 atm. What is the solubility of $\ce{O2}$ in water exposed to ordinary air, in which oxygen's partial pressure is 0.21 atm?
:::
::: tab Answer
Henry's law: dissolved concentration is proportional to the gas's partial pressure.

$$k_\text{H} = \frac{c}{P} = \frac{1.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{M}}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 1.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{M/atm}$$

$$c = k_\text{H}P = (1.3\times10^{-3})(0.21) = 2.7\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}$$

**Why this number matters.** Water in contact with air holds only about 0.3 millimoles of oxygen per liter — roughly 9 mg/L. That thin supply is what every fish in a river is breathing, and it is why a rise of a few degrees in water temperature (which lowers gas solubility further) can be lethal to aquatic life even though nothing toxic has been added.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2a}} · *workout* What are the mole fractions of $\ce{H3PO4}$ and water in a solution made from 14.5 g of $\ce{H3PO4}$ dissolved in 125 g of water? What is the molality?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$14.5\ \text{g}\ \ce{H3PO4}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{98.0\ \text{g}} = 0.148\ \text{mol}\ \ce{H3PO4}$$

$$125\ \text{g}\ \ce{H2O}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.0\ \text{g}} = 6.94\ \text{mol}\ \ce{H2O}$$

$$X_{\ce{H3PO4}} = \frac{0.148}{0.148+6.94} = 0.0209 \qquad X_{\ce{H2O}} = 1-0.0209 = 0.979$$

$$m = \frac{0.148\ \text{mol}}{0.125\ \text{kg}} = 1.18\ \text{mol/kg}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2a}} · *workout* Concentrated nitric acid is sold as a solution that is 68.0% $\ce{HNO3}$ by mass. What are the mole fractions of $\ce{HNO3}$ and water?
:::
::: tab Answer
Assume exactly 100 g of solution: 68.0 g $\ce{HNO3}$ and 32.0 g water.

$$68.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{HNO3}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{63.0\ \text{g}} = 1.079\ \text{mol}\ \ce{HNO3}$$

$$32.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{H2O}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.0\ \text{g}} = 1.778\ \text{mol}\ \ce{H2O}$$

$$X_{\ce{HNO3}} = \frac{1.079}{1.079+1.778} = 0.378 \qquad X_{\ce{H2O}} = 0.622$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2a}} · *workout* A solution is made by dissolving 25.0 g of glucose ($\ce{C6H12O6}$, 180.16 g/mol) in 175 g of water. Calculate (a) the percent by mass of glucose, (b) the molality, and \(c) the mole fraction of glucose.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$n_\text{glucose} = \frac{25.0\ \text{g}}{180.16\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.1388\ \text{mol} \qquad n_{\ce{H2O}} = \frac{175\ \text{g}}{18.02\ \text{g/mol}} = 9.712\ \text{mol}$$

**(a) Percent by mass.** The mass of solution is 25.0 + 175 = 200. g:
$$\frac{25.0}{200.}\times100\% = 12.5\%$$

**(b) Molality.** Divide by the mass of *solvent* in kg:
$$m = \frac{0.1388\ \text{mol}}{0.175\ \text{kg}} = 0.793\ \text{mol/kg}$$

**\(c) Mole fraction.**
$$X_\text{glucose} = \frac{0.1388}{0.1388 + 9.712} = 0.0141$$

Notice that no density was given and none was needed — all three of these units are composition-based. Only molarity would have required one.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2b}} · *workout* A solution of hydrochloric acid is 6.00 m and has a density of 1.10 g/mL. What is its molarity? (Molar mass of $\ce{HCl}$ = 36.5 g/mol.)
:::
::: tab Answer
Assume 1 kg (1000 g) of water, giving 6.00 mol $\ce{HCl}$.

$$\text{mass of}\ \ce{HCl} = 6.00\ \text{mol}\times\frac{36.5\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 219\ \text{g}$$

$$\text{mass of solution} = 219\ \text{g} + 1000\ \text{g} = 1219\ \text{g}$$

$$\text{volume of solution} = \frac{1219\ \text{g}}{1.10\ \text{g/mL}} = 1108\ \text{mL} = 1.108\ \text{L}$$

$$M = \frac{6.00\ \text{mol}}{1.108\ \text{L}} = 5.42\ \text{mol/L}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2b}} · *workout* An aqueous solution of ethanol ($\ce{C2H5OH}$, 46.07 g/mol) is 40.0% ethanol by mass and has a density of 0.947 g/mL. Calculate its molarity and its molality.
:::
::: tab Answer
Percent by mass is given, so **assume 100 g of solution**: 40.0 g ethanol and 60.0 g water.

$$n_\text{ethanol} = \frac{40.0\ \text{g}}{46.07\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.868\ \text{mol}$$

**Molarity** needs the volume, which is where the density comes in:
$$V = \frac{100\ \text{g}}{0.947\ \text{g/mL}} = 105.6\ \text{mL} = 0.1056\ \text{L} \qquad M = \frac{0.868}{0.1056} = 8.22\ \text{M}$$

**Molality** needs the mass of solvent alone — the 60.0 g of water:
$$m = \frac{0.868\ \text{mol}}{0.0600\ \text{kg}} = 14.5\ \text{mol/kg}$$

**The two numbers differ by 76%,** which is worth pausing on. In dilute aqueous solutions molarity and molality nearly coincide; here, with 40% of the mass being solute and the density well below 1 g/mL, they do not come close. Never substitute one for the other without checking how concentrated the solution is.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 12.2b}} · *multiple-choice* A solution is warmed from 20 °C to 60 °C in a sealed container. Which of its concentration measures changes?

(A) Molality only
(B) Molarity only
\(C) Both molarity and molality
(D) Neither
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B) Molarity only.** Sealing the container means no solute and no solvent leaves, so every *amount* is unchanged: moles of solute, mass of solvent, and total moles all stay exactly as they were. Mole fraction, percent by mass, and molality are therefore all unchanged.

Molarity is the exception because its denominator is a **volume**, and liquids expand on heating. The same moles now occupy a slightly larger volume, so the molarity falls slightly.

This is precisely the reason $K_b$ and $K_f$ are defined using molality: a boiling-point calculation happens at the boiling point, where a molarity determined at room temperature would no longer be correct.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3a}} · *workout* A solution contains 5.00 g of urea, $\ce{CO(NH2)2}$ (nonvolatile), dissolved in 0.100 kg of water. The vapor pressure of pure water at 25 °C is 23.7 torr. What is the vapor pressure of the solution?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$5.00\ \text{g urea}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{60.0\ \text{g}} = 0.0833\ \text{mol urea}$$

$$100\ \text{g water}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.0\ \text{g}} = 5.56\ \text{mol water}$$

$$X_{\ce{H2O}} = \frac{5.56}{5.56+0.0833} = 0.985$$

$$P = 0.985\times 23.7\ \text{torr} = 23.3\ \text{torr}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3a}} · *workout* At 30 °C the vapor pressure of pure water is 31.8 torr. What is the vapor pressure of a solution containing 45.0 g of glycerol ($\ce{C3H8O3}$, 92.09 g/mol, nonvolatile) in 150. g of water?
:::
::: tab Answer
Raoult's law needs the mole fraction of the **solvent**, so both components must be converted to moles.

$$n_\text{glycerol} = \frac{45.0}{92.09} = 0.4887\ \text{mol} \qquad n_{\ce{H2O}} = \frac{150.}{18.02} = 8.324\ \text{mol}$$

$$X_{\ce{H2O}} = \frac{8.324}{8.324 + 0.4887} = 0.9446$$

$$P = X_{\ce{H2O}}P^0 = (0.9446)(31.8\ \text{torr}) = 30.0\ \text{torr}$$

{{sp[warning] The most common slip}} Using the mole fraction of the *solute* (0.0554) instead of the solvent gives 1.76 torr — an answer that says a 5% solution has almost no vapor pressure at all. Raoult's law is written for the component whose vapor you are asking about, and here that is the water.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3a}} · *short answer* Raoult's law is stated for an ideal solution. What does "ideal" mean here, and would you expect a solution of ethanol in water to obey it closely? Explain.
:::
::: tab Answer
**"Ideal" means the solute-solvent attractions are the same strength as the solvent-solvent and solute-solute attractions they replace.** If that holds, a solvent molecule at the surface is equally likely to escape whether its neighbors are solvent or solute, and vapor pressure depends only on how many solvent molecules occupy the surface — which is exactly what $P_1 = X_1P_1^0$ says.

**Ethanol and water deviate noticeably.** The two hydrogen-bond with each other, but not in quite the same way or with quite the same strength as each does with itself, and mixing them measurably changes the total. The mixture shows a **positive deviation** — the real vapor pressure runs above Raoult's prediction — and the deviation is large enough to produce an azeotrope at about 95% ethanol, which is why simple distillation cannot produce pure ethanol.

**The general rule:** Raoult's law is most reliable for **dilute** solutions and for components chemically similar to one another. It is a limiting law, in the same way the ideal gas law is.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3b}} · *workout* What is the boiling point of a solution of 9.04 g of $\ce{I2}$ (nonvolatile) dissolved in 75.5 g of benzene? The normal boiling point of benzene is 80.1 °C, and $K_b$ for benzene is 2.53 °C/m.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$9.04\ \text{g}\ \ce{I2}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{253.8\ \text{g}} = 0.0356\ \text{mol}\ \ce{I2}$$

$$m = \frac{0.0356\ \text{mol}}{0.0755\ \text{kg}} = 0.472\ \text{mol/kg}$$

$$\Delta T_b = K_bm = 2.53\ \text{°C/m}\times 0.472\ \text{m} = 1.19\ \text{°C}$$

New boiling point $= 80.1\ \text{°C} + 1.19\ \text{°C} = 81.3\ \text{°C}$.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3b}} · *short answer* Two aqueous solutions have the same molality, 0.02 mol/kg: one is table sugar (a nonvolatile molecular compound), the other is table salt, $\ce{NaCl}$. Which solution has the higher boiling point? Why?
:::
::: tab Answer
The **$\ce{NaCl}$ solution**. Sugar is a nonelectrolyte ($i=1$), while $\ce{NaCl}$ dissociates into two ions per formula unit ($i\approx 2$), roughly doubling the effective particle concentration and therefore roughly doubling the boiling-point elevation compared to the sugar solution at the same molality.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3b}} · *workout* A 2.50 g sample of an unknown nonelectrolyte is dissolved in 45.0 g of benzene, lowering the freezing point from 5.50 °C to 4.28 °C. What is the molar mass of the unknown? ($K_f$ of benzene $= 5.12\ \text{°C/m}$.)
:::
::: tab Answer
Freezing-point depression run backwards is a classic molar-mass determination.

**Step 1 — the depression.**
$$\Delta T_f = 5.50 - 4.28 = 1.22\ \text{°C}$$

**Step 2 — solve for molality.**
$$m = \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f} = \frac{1.22}{5.12} = 0.2383\ \text{mol/kg}$$

**Step 3 — moles of solute in the sample.** Molality is per kg of *solvent*, and there are 0.0450 kg of benzene:
$$n = (0.2383\ \text{mol/kg})(0.0450\ \text{kg}) = 1.072\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$$

**Step 4 — molar mass.**
$$\mathcal{M} = \frac{2.50\ \text{g}}{1.072\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol}} = 233\ \text{g/mol}$$

Benzene is the traditional solvent for this measurement because its $K_f$ (5.12) is nearly three times water's (1.86), so the same solute produces a nearly threefold larger — and therefore more precisely measurable — temperature change.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3c}} · *workout* A 100.0 mL solution contains 0.103 g of bovine insulin (molar mass 5700 g/mol). What is its osmotic pressure at 18 °C, assuming ideal solution behavior?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$0.103\ \text{g}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{5700\ \text{g}} = 1.81\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol}$$

$$M = \frac{1.81\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol}}{0.1000\ \text{L}} = 1.81\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}$$

$$\pi = MRT = 1.81\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}\times 0.0821\ \frac{\text{L·atm}}{\text{mol·K}}\times (18+273)\ \text{K} = 4.32\times10^{-3}\ \text{atm}$$

This tiny but measurable pressure is exactly why osmotic pressure — not freezing-point depression — is the preferred method for determining the molar mass of large biomolecules like proteins.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3c}} · *short answer* A freshwater fish placed in seawater dies, and a saltwater fish placed in fresh water also dies. Explain both outcomes in terms of osmosis.
:::
::: tab Answer
Osmosis always moves solvent **toward the more concentrated solution**, and a cell membrane is a semipermeable membrane.

**Freshwater fish in seawater.** Seawater is far more concentrated in dissolved salts than the fish's cells. Water therefore flows *out* of the cells and into the surrounding seawater. The cells shrivel and dehydrate — the fish dies of water loss while completely surrounded by water.

**Saltwater fish in fresh water.** Now the fish's cells are the more concentrated side. Water flows *into* the cells, which swell and can rupture.

**Why the same principle explains both:** neither outcome depends on salt being harmful. It depends only on which side of the membrane has more dissolved particles, since that is the only thing osmosis responds to. The same reasoning is why intravenous fluids must be **isotonic** with blood — pure water into a vein would burst red blood cells.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3c}} · *workout* What is the osmotic pressure at 25 °C of a solution containing 12.0 g of sucrose ($\ce{C12H22O11}$, 342.3 g/mol) in enough water to make 250. mL of solution?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$n = \frac{12.0\ \text{g}}{342.3\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.03506\ \text{mol}$$

$$M = \frac{0.03506\ \text{mol}}{0.250\ \text{L}} = 0.1402\ \text{M}$$

$$\pi = MRT = (0.1402)(0.0821)(298) = 3.43\ \text{atm}$$

Sucrose is a nonelectrolyte, so $i = 1$ and no correction is needed. Note the size of the result: 3.4 atm from 12 g of table sugar — more than three times atmospheric pressure. Osmotic pressure is by far the largest of the four colligative effects for a given concentration, which is both why it is useful for measurement and why osmotic balance is something living cells must control tightly.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3d}} · *workout* Calculate the freezing-point depression of a 0.15 m aqueous $\ce{CaCl2}$ solution. ($K_f$ of water = 1.86 °C/m.)
:::
::: tab Answer
$\ce{CaCl2}$ dissociates as $\ce{CaCl2 -> Ca^2+ + 2Cl-}$, giving $i = 3$.

$$\Delta T_f = iK_fm = 3\times 1.86\ \text{°C/m}\times 0.15\ \text{m} = 0.837\ \text{°C}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3d}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following solutes, at equal molality in water, would produce the *largest* freezing-point depression?

(A) Glucose, $\ce{C6H12O6}$ ($i=1$)
(B) $\ce{NaCl}$ ($i\approx 2$)
\(C) $\ce{K3PO4}$ ($i\approx 4$)
(D) They would all be equal
:::
::: tab Answer
**\(C) $\ce{K3PO4}$.** It dissociates into 4 ions per formula unit ($\ce{3K+ + PO4^3-}$), giving the largest van't Hoff factor and therefore the largest $\Delta T_f = iK_fm$ at equal molality.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 27
{{sp[info] Objective 12.3d}} · *short answer* An intravenous saline drip is 0.15 M $\ce{NaCl}$. A glucose drip is 0.30 M glucose. Explain why both are safe to infuse, even though one is twice the molarity of the other.
:::
::: tab Answer
Colligative properties respond to **particles**, not to formula units, so compare the two on that basis.

$$\ce{NaCl -> Na+ + Cl-} \quad i = 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (0.15\ \text{M})(2) = 0.30\ \text{M particles}$$
$$\text{glucose does not dissociate} \quad i = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad (0.30\ \text{M})(1) = 0.30\ \text{M particles}$$

Both deliver **0.30 M of dissolved particles**, which is why both produce the same osmotic pressure and both are **isotonic** with blood plasma. A red blood cell placed in either one neither swells nor shrivels.

**The general lesson:** the molarity printed on a label tells you about the compound; multiplying by $i$ tells you what the solution actually does. For any colligative comparison, convert to particles first.
:::
::::
